questions.question_stem: What does each block's header hold that makes the blocks form a chain?
questions.correct_answer: The hash of the block before it, which is what links each block to the last.
incorrect_answers: The signature of the miner before it, which is what links each block to the last.
The private key of the block before it, which is what links each block to the last.
The full copy of the block before it, which is what links each block to the last.
questions.explanation: A block's header holds the hash of the block before it, so each block points back to the one before and the blocks form one chain back to the first.
questions.lesson_block: A blockchain is blocks, each linked to the last
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/introduction/02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: A blockchain is blocks, each linked to the last

questions.question_stem: A node receives a payment that claims to spend Alice's coin. Which check shows that Alice authorized it?
questions.correct_answer: That its signature unlocks the coin being spent, since only the key holder can make one.
incorrect_answers: That the outputs add up to no more than the inputs, since only the owner can balance them.
That the first node to relay it was Alice's own, since only her node would send her payment.
That a miner has already put it in a block, since only the real owner can ever ask for it.
questions.explanation: Each node checks that the signature unlocks the coin being spent, that the coin is still unspent, and that the outputs do not add up to more than the inputs. Only the signature check shows who authorized the payment; the others check the coin and the amounts.
questions.lesson_block: Nodes check a payment before passing it on
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/introduction/02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: Nodes check a payment before passing it on

questions.question_stem: An agent writes that a suspect moved "USDT". What else must you know before you can look the payment up?
questions.correct_answer: You need the chain too: USDT sits on several chains, such as Tron and Ethereum, and each keeps its own separate record of payments.
incorrect_answers: You need the exchange too: USDT moves only between accounts, and the exchange keeps the one record of each payment, not a chain.
You need the wallet too: USDT is a coin that lives inside a wallet, and the wallet app keeps the record that an explorer can read.
You need the miner too: USDT payments are written into blocks by miners, and each miner keeps a different record of each payment.
questions.explanation: A cryptocurrency is one asset a chain records, and one asset can sit on many chains. As of 31 Oct 2026, 51% of USDT was on Tron and 39% on Ethereum, each chain with its own record and explorer. Name both: "USDT on Tron", not "crypto".
questions.lesson_block: A blockchain is a record, not a currency
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/introduction/02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: A blockchain is a record, not a currency

questions.question_stem: A transaction has been broadcast and relayed by several nodes, but it has not yet appeared in a block. What is the best interpretation of its status?
questions.correct_answer: It is valid enough to be pending in the mempool, but it is not finalized on the chain yet.
incorrect_answers: It is confirmed once enough peers have relayed it, before a block is chosen by consensus.
It is already in the ledger, but later confirmations have not accumulated on top of it.
It is waiting for a wallet signature, because relay comes before authorization checks.
questions.explanation: Nodes hold a valid payment that is waiting for a block in a mempool, kept in memory. "Unconfirmed" on an explorer means seen, not settled: a payment that is never mined fades as nodes restart.
questions.lesson_block: Unconfirmed is not paid: it can still vanish
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/introduction/02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: Unconfirmed is not paid: it can still vanish

questions.question_stem: Which order describes the five steps of Alice's payment, from her wallet to the chain?
questions.correct_answer: Sign it, broadcast it to nodes, hold it in the mempool, mine it into a block, then count confirmations on top.
incorrect_answers: Sign it, mine it into a block, broadcast the block to nodes, hold it in the mempool, then count the confirmations.
Broadcast it to nodes, sign it, hold it in the mempool, count confirmations, then mine it into a block.
Sign it, hold it in the mempool, broadcast it to nodes, count confirmations, then mine it into a block last.
questions.explanation: Every payment takes the same five steps: it is signed, broadcast to nodes, held in the mempool, included in a block, and then confirmed as blocks pile on top.
questions.lesson_block: Every payment takes the same five steps
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/introduction/02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: Every payment takes the same five steps

questions.question_stem: An attacker changes a transaction in an old block. Why does this disrupt the chain rather than remaining a hidden edit?
questions.correct_answer: Changing the old block changes its hash, which breaks the hash link expected by later blocks.
incorrect_answers: Changing the old block changes its timestamp, which later blocks use as their pointer in validation.
Changing the old block changes its Merkle root, so later transaction signatures must be recreated.
Changing the old block changes its block height, so nodes cannot locate later transactions by height.
questions.explanation: Hash links make the ledger tamper-evident: if earlier data changes, its digital fingerprint changes, so later blocks no longer point cleanly to the expected prior block.
questions.lesson_block: A blockchain is blocks, each linked to the last
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/introduction/02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: A blockchain is blocks, each linked to the last

questions.question_stem: A student looks for "Alice's balance" stored in a Bitcoin block and cannot find one. Why?
questions.correct_answer: Bitcoin stores unspent outputs, not balances; a wallet or explorer adds up the outputs its keys can spend.
incorrect_answers: Bitcoin stores one account per address, but explorers hide the balance field for privacy reasons alone, by rule.
Bitcoin stores balances in the block header, but only the miner who built the block is able to read them.
Bitcoin stores balances off the chain in wallets, and each wallet sends its balance to nodes when asked.
questions.explanation: The chain stores unspent outputs, and a payment spends whole outputs and makes change. A balance is added up by a wallet or explorer from the outputs its keys can spend; Ethereum and the course chain do store balances.
questions.lesson_block: Bitcoin keeps no balances, only unspent coins
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/introduction/02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: Bitcoin keeps no balances, only unspent coins

questions.question_stem: A user says their public blockchain activity is completely anonymous because their wallet address is not their legal name. What is the most accurate correction?
questions.correct_answer: Public chain activity is pseudonymous; if the address is linked to the person, its public history can become traceable.
incorrect_answers: Public chain activity is private as long as users rotate addresses, because transaction links disappear from analysis.
Public chain activity is anonymous until a block explorer indexes it, then only miners can trace the activity.
Public chain activity is confidential because validators see addresses but not the payment graph behind them.
questions.explanation: Bitcoin is pseudonymous, not anonymous. Every payment is public, and once one address is tied to a person, its history is exposed.
questions.lesson_block: Four beliefs to correct when you brief
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/introduction/02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: Four beliefs to correct when you brief

questions.question_stem: An explorer page for a Bitcoin payment shows the txid, a fee and an "Exchange" tag. How should you treat each?
questions.correct_answer: The txid is chain data, the fee is worked out from earlier transactions, and the tag is a lead: Low on its own.
incorrect_answers: The txid, the fee and the tag are all chain data, because an explorer only ever repeats what the node holds on file.
The txid and the tag are chain data, but the fee is a guess, because no node can work out what was paid.
The fee and the tag are chain data, but the txid is the explorer's own label for a payment that it has seen.
questions.explanation: An explorer shows what a node holds (txid, outputs, block), plus figures it works out (input amounts, fee) and labels it adds. A tag alone is Low confidence: a lead, not a fact.
questions.lesson_block: An explorer is a node's record, plus extras
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/introduction/02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: An explorer is a node's record, plus extras

questions.question_stem: A team claims that because blockchain signatures and hashes are strong, users cannot lose assets to attacks. Which response is most accurate?
questions.correct_answer: Strong core cryptography does not eliminate endpoint risks such as wallet compromise, phishing, exchanges, or smart contract bugs.
incorrect_answers: Strong signatures also secure wallet apps and exchanges, so asset loss usually means the underlying cryptography failed, not user systems.
Endpoint compromise matters only before broadcast; once signed, network consensus can label a transfer fraudulent later.
Phishing is mainly a privacy issue, because it reveals addresses but cannot cause a valid asset transfer without breaking cryptography.
questions.explanation: The cryptography is strong. Thefts happen at the endpoints: wallets and exchanges.
questions.lesson_block: Four beliefs to correct when you brief
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/introduction/02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: Four beliefs to correct when you brief

questions.question_stem: Alice's Bitcoin wallet selects one prior unspent output worth more than her purchase. Why might the resulting transaction include an output back to Alice?
questions.correct_answer: Bitcoin inputs are spent whole, so the wallet creates a change output for leftover value not paid to Bob or used as a fee.
incorrect_answers: Bitcoin requires a return output as proof Alice controlled the spent output before peers relay it across the network.
The wallet is creating an explicit miner-fee output first, then refunding any unused fee amount back to Alice inside the transaction.
Bob's wallet adds the output after broadcast so the extra value from Alice's larger input is not lost when nodes confirm it.
questions.explanation: The reading explains the UTXO model: transactions consume previous outputs and create new outputs, often including ordinary change outputs because inputs are indivisible.
questions.specific_source_reading: /tmp/reading-02-ch02.adoc: Transaction Inputs and Outputs; Making Change; Coin Selection

questions.question_stem: A simplified Bitcoin transaction consumes inputs totaling 1.00 BTC and creates outputs totaling 0.995 BTC. What happens to the remaining 0.005 BTC?
questions.correct_answer: It is the implied transaction fee available to the miner who includes the transaction in a valid block.
incorrect_answers: It stays in the original UTXO for Alice to spend later because inputs can be partly spent by design.
It becomes a required miner output that the wallet must list alongside the payment outputs in the transaction.
It is returned to Alice by peer nodes after confirmation if no separate change output exists in the transaction.
questions.explanation: The reading states that transaction fees are implicit: the fee is the difference between total input value and total output value, not a separate required output.
questions.specific_source_reading: /tmp/reading-02-ch02.adoc: Transaction Inputs and Outputs; Creating the Outputs

questions.question_stem: Bob sees Alice's Bitcoin transaction reach the network within seconds. Why does waiting for additional confirmations give Bob stronger settlement confidence?
questions.correct_answer: Each later block built on top of the transaction's block adds proof of work an attacker would need to replace.
incorrect_answers: Each later block gives Bob another signed receipt from Alice's wallet, so authorization becomes stronger with time.
Each later block moves the payment through more mempools, so enough relay eventually becomes settlement.
Each later block locks the transaction by encrypting older data, making previous blocks unreadable to attackers.
questions.explanation: The reading treats confirmations as accumulated proof-of-work security: reversal becomes increasingly costly as more blocks build on top of the block containing the transaction.
